problems.title: A router that picks an open-source model per query, cheaper than always-largest
problems.problem: Given a pool of open-weights models (say 3-5, differing in cost and strength) and a stream of queries, pick for each query the cheapest model that still passes. The reference point is the trivial strategy: always the largest model. The router has to be substantially cheaper than that at comparable quality. A submission must contain working code and a way to reproduce the numbers.

acceptance.how: The repo contains `make eval`, which on a public query set named in the repo prints JSON: {accuracy, cost_usd, n}. A stranger clones the repo, runs one command and gets the same numbers (+/- noise, documented in the README). The verifier sends cost_usd alone as the score and confirms that accuracy did not drop below 98% of the baseline; if it did, that is a mismatch.
acceptance.metric: cost_usd - total cost of the run in USD

problems.title: Compression judged by the next action, not by the text
problems.problem:
Compressors are scored against the original text: overlap, similarity, human ratings. An agent never reads the text. It reads a tool output and then does something. So score the thing that matters: compress a tool output, hand it to the agent instead of the original, and check whether the next tool call is the same one.
The interesting failures are not fluency. They are the deletions that read as harmless and are not: an identifier, a negation, a quantifier, a unit. A compressor can score well on similarity and still change what the agent does next.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make eval` over a public set of agent traces named in the README (each trace: a tool output plus the call the agent actually made next). For every trace it compresses the output, replays the turn against the compressed version, and prints JSON: {reduction, action_fidelity, n}. reduction is the fraction of input tokens removed, measured with the tokenizer named in the README.
A verifier clones the repo, runs one command and sends action_fidelity as the score. It counts only if reduction >= 0.50 on the same run; below that, send verdict "mismatch" and say so in the output.
acceptance.metric: action_fidelity - percent of turns where the next tool call, name and arguments, is byte identical to the uncompressed run, at >= 50 percent token reduction

problems.title: A repo digest that beats reading the files, at the same context budget
problems.problem:
Point an agent at an unfamiliar repository and it burns most of its budget finding out what is where. The usual answer is a digest: compile the repository once into a compact artifact and give the agent that instead.
Nobody publishes the comparison that matters. A digest is only worth its tokens if it beats spending the SAME number of tokens on raw file content picked by a plain search. Beat that baseline, on questions whose answers can be checked.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make eval` against a public repository at a pinned commit and a question set, both named in the README. Questions must have checkable answers: which file defines X, what calls Y, which module owns Z. It builds a digest of at most 8000 tokens, answers every question from the digest alone, and prints JSON: {accuracy, digest_tokens, n, baseline_accuracy}.
baseline_accuracy is the same question set answered from 8000 tokens of raw file content selected by grep, and your repo has to run that arm too. A verifier sends accuracy as the score and checks that digest_tokens <= 8000 and accuracy > baseline_accuracy; if the baseline wins, that is verdict "mismatch".
acceptance.metric: accuracy - percent of questions answered correctly from a digest of at most 8000 tokens

problems.title: Catch a confidently wrong answer for less than it costs to generate it again
problems.problem:
A model that is wrong and sure of itself is the expensive failure: nothing downstream flags it. The known defences all cost about as much as the answer did. Sample it five times and vote, or ask a bigger model, and you have paid several times over for a check.
The open question is whether a check can be much cheaper than generation and still catch most of the confident errors, without flagging so many correct answers that nobody keeps it switched on.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make eval` over a public task set with known answers, named in the README. For every task it generates an answer, runs your check, and prints JSON: {caught, false_alarms, cost_ratio, n}. caught is the percent of WRONG answers your check flags. false_alarms is the percent of CORRECT answers it flags. cost_ratio is the cost of checking divided by the cost of generating, both measured on the same run.
A verifier sends caught as the score and confirms cost_ratio <= 0.25 and false_alarms <= 5 on the same run. Either constraint broken is verdict "mismatch": a check that flags everything catches everything and is worth nothing.
acceptance.metric: caught - percent of wrong answers flagged, at a cost ratio of at most 0.25 and at most 5 percent false alarms

problems.title: Make a public test suite run twice as fast without skipping a single test
problems.problem:
Slow test suites are paid for on every commit by everyone on the project, and the usual speedups are cheating: skip the slow ones, drop to a smaller matrix, mark the flaky ones as expected failures. That is not a faster suite, it is a smaller one.
Take a real public repository with a suite that takes minutes, and make it finish in half the time with exactly the same tests running and exactly the same ones passing.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README a public repository and a pinned commit. Your repo runs `make bench`, which runs the suite three times on a clean checkout and prints JSON: {seconds_median, tests_run, tests_passed, baseline_seconds_median}. The baseline arm is the untouched upstream suite on the same machine in the same run, so the number does not depend on whose laptop it was.
A verifier clones, runs one command and sends seconds_median as the score. tests_run and tests_passed must equal the baseline arm exactly; one test fewer is verdict "mismatch". Tolerance is wide here on purpose: wall clock is noisy.
acceptance.metric: seconds_median - median wall clock of the full suite over three runs, in seconds

problems.title: Reorder a prompt so most of it is served from cache, with the answers unchanged
problems.problem:
Providers bill a cached prefix at a fraction of the normal input price, and the cache only holds while the beginning of the prompt is byte identical. Most prompts are assembled in the order a human found readable, so a timestamp, a session id or a shuffled tool list lands near the front and throws the discount away.
The task is mechanical and the payoff is immediate: rearrange the prompt so the stable part comes first and the volatile part last, without changing a single answer.

acceptance.how:
Your repo runs `make eval` over a fixed set of at least 50 prompts named in the README, twice in a row against one provider. It prints JSON: {cache_read_fraction, answers_identical, n}. cache_read_fraction is cached input tokens divided by all input tokens, taken from the provider usage fields, not estimated.
A verifier sends cache_read_fraction as the score and confirms answers_identical equals n on the same run. One changed answer is verdict "mismatch": this is a reordering, not a rewrite.
acceptance.metric: cache_read_fraction - cached input tokens divided by total input tokens over the whole run

problems.title: Cut a container image to a third of its size with the application still working
problems.problem:
Container images ship a whole build environment to production: compilers, package caches, documentation, sometimes a second copy of the runtime. Everyone knows the fix and almost nobody measures it, so images that could be tens of megabytes are hundreds, and every pull, every scale up and every cold start pays for it.
Take a public application with a fat official image and make it small, with its own smoke test still green.

acceptance.how:
Name in your README a public application and a pinned version. Your repo runs `make image` to build it and `make smoke` to run the application's OWN smoke test, not one you wrote, against the built image. It prints JSON: {image_mb, smoke_passed, baseline_mb}, where image_mb is the uncompressed size reported by the container runtime and baseline_mb is the official image measured the same way.
A verifier builds it themselves and sends image_mb as the score. smoke_passed must be true and image_mb must be at most one third of baseline_mb; otherwise verdict "mismatch".
acceptance.metric: image_mb - uncompressed size of the final image in megabytes
